title: Inclusive and Special Needs Education
summary: Learn to teach every learner: rights and models of disability, understanding diverse needs, Universal Design for Learning, differentiation and exam accommodations, individual support plans, positive behaviour support and assistive technology.
audience: Teachers, teaching assistants, school leaders, parents and education students

body.p: Inclusive education means all learners, including those with disabilities and other additional needs, learn together in ordinary schools with the support they need. It is a right under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Article 24) and part of Sustainable Development Goal 4.

UNICEF estimates that nearly 240 million children worldwide, about 1 in 10, have a disability. A typical class of 40 might therefore include about 4 learners with disabilities, as well as others with learning difficulties, language barriers or emotional needs.

list: Medical model: disability is a problem in the person to be fixed or treated.
Social model: people are disabled mainly by barriers in society, such as inaccessible buildings, rigid teaching and negative attitudes, so the task is to remove barriers.

body.p: Inclusion uses the social model: instead of asking "what is wrong with this child?", ask "what is stopping this child from learning, and how can we change it?" Inclusive practices usually benefit all learners, not only those with identified needs.

body.tip: Many countries have inclusive-education policies; learn yours, for example South Africa's Education White Paper 6 or national special-needs policies elsewhere.

body.p: Teachers do not diagnose, but they notice difficulties early and work with families and specialists. Common areas of need include:

list: Specific learning difficulties: dyslexia (reading and spelling), dyscalculia (number), dysgraphia (writing).
Attention and activity: ADHD can affect concentration, organisation and impulse control.
Autism: differences in social communication and sensory processing, often with strong interests and a preference for routine.
Sensory impairments: low vision or blindness, hearing loss or deafness.
Physical disabilities affecting movement or fine motor skills.
Intellectual disabilities affecting learning across areas.
Speech and language difficulties.
Social, emotional and mental health needs, often linked to life circumstances.

body.p: Each learner is an individual: two learners with the same label may need very different support. Talk with the learner and their family about strengths, interests and what helps.

body.tip: Simple screening helps: check whether a struggling learner can see the board and hear clearly before assuming a learning difficulty.

body.p: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) plans lessons from the start so that as many learners as possible can access them, rather than adapting afterwards. It has three principles:

list: Multiple means of engagement: offer choices, relevance and different ways to stay motivated.
Multiple means of representation: present information in several ways, such as speech, text, pictures, objects, demonstrations and video with captions.
Multiple means of action and expression: let learners show what they know in different ways, such as writing, speaking, drawing, building or using technology.
Write key words on the board and say them aloud.
Use real objects and pictures, especially for new vocabulary.
Break tasks into small steps with clear instructions.
Allow pair work so learners support each other.
Provide a quiet corner and predictable routines.
Offer worked examples alongside open challenges.

body.tip: Start with one UDL change per lesson, such as adding a visual for every key idea, and build from there.

body.p: Differentiation adapts teaching to learners' readiness, interests and needs, while keeping high expectations for everyone.

list: Content: what learners work on, such as simpler texts on the same topic.
Process: how they learn, such as extra examples, manipulatives or peer support.
Product: how they show learning, such as an oral answer instead of writing.
Environment: seating near the front for a learner with low vision, or away from noise for one easily distracted.

body.p: Reasonable adjustments let learners show what they know without lowering the standard. Common examples include extra time, a reader or scribe, large print, rest breaks or a separate room. With 25% extra time, a 2-hour (120-minute) exam becomes 150 minutes; a 90-minute test becomes 112.5 minutes. Exam bodies set their own rules and require applications in advance.

body.tip: Accommodations should change how learning is accessed or shown, not what is being assessed.

body.p: Learners with significant needs benefit from an individual education or support plan (IEP or ISP). It records strengths, needs, specific goals, the support to be provided, who provides it and when progress will be reviewed.
Make goals specific and measurable: "By the end of term, Thabo will read and understand a short paragraph of 50 familiar words with 90% accuracy" is better than "Thabo will improve his reading".

list: Families know the child best and must be partners in planning.
Learners themselves should take part in planning as far as possible.
School-based support teams, learning-support teachers and assistants share strategies.
Specialists (therapists, psychologists, health workers) advise on specific needs.
District support services may provide assistive devices or specialist placements when needed.

body.tip: Review plans regularly and keep them short and practical; a plan nobody uses helps no one.

lessons.title: Positive behaviour support and assistive technology

body.p: Behaviour is communication. Distress, avoidance or disruption often signals that a learner cannot cope with a task, environment or situation. Positive behaviour support looks for the reasons and teaches better ways to meet the need.

list: Set clear, positive expectations and consistent routines.
Notice and praise appropriate behaviour specifically.
Identify triggers (noise, transitions, difficult tasks) and reduce them.
Teach calming strategies and give safe ways to ask for a break.
Avoid humiliation and physical punishment, which harm learning and are banned in many countries.

body.p: Assistive technology helps learners access learning: magnifiers and large print, screen readers and text-to-speech, hearing aids and captioning, speech-to-text, communication boards and apps, adapted keyboards and simple low-tech supports such as pencil grips and sloping boards. Many phones and computers include accessibility features at no extra cost.

body.tip: Learn the accessibility settings on the devices your school already has; they are often unused.
